We also record the volume--normalized flow, for which the Bures--Helstrom metric is a fixed point. Its linearization is the shifted round--sphere Laplacian [MATH], with spectrum \sigma_\ell=-(\ell-1)(\ell+3), and spectral gap [MATH] after removal of the scaling mode.
tldr: This paper studies the Ricci flow of the Bures-Helstrom metric on the qubit state space, showing it is a homothetic shrinker and analyzing its properties.
motivation: To understand the geometric flow of a monotone Riemannian metric on quantum state space, which is relevant to quantum information geometry but not directly to the user's core interests.
method: The authors derive the Ricci flow equations in a rotationally symmetric gauge, use a Hamilton-DeTurck gauge choice to simplify, and analyze the resulting PDEs.
result: The Bures-Helstrom metric is an Einstein metric, and its Ricci flow is a homothetic shrinker with explicit extinction time; the volume-normalized flow has the metric as a fixed point with a shifted round-sphere Laplacian linearization.
conclusion: The metric remains inside the monotone cone until the collapsed limit, and the study provides explicit geometric evolution equations.

title: A Land Of Monotone Plenty, Bis Repetita: From Classical To Weak Optimal Transport
authors: Virginie Ehrlacher, Rodrigue Lelotte, Luca Nenna
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The celebrated c-cyclical monotonicity property is shown to boil down to the zeroth-order optimality condition for the optimal transport problem. More precisely, we show that optimality is equivalent to the non-negativity of the linear transport cost functional on the radial cone of admissible perturbations. We then utilise this point of view to extend the c-cyclical monotonicity property to the weak optimal transport problem, for which it corresponds to the first-order optimality condition, namely to the non-negativity of the linearisation of the weak transport cost functional near the optimiser. Altogether, this sheds new light on this monotonicity concept. For both classical and weak optimal transport, we show that this property characterises (under suitable assumptions) optimal transport plans. In the classical case, we recover known results of the literature but with revisited proofs.
tldr: This paper extends the concept of c-cyclical monotonicity from classical optimal transport to weak optimal transport, showing it corresponds to first-order optimality conditions.
motivation: To generalize the monotonicity property that characterizes optimal transport plans to the weak optimal transport setting, providing a unified perspective.
method: The authors reformulate optimality in classical transport as non-negativity of a linear functional on a radial cone, then extend this viewpoint to weak transport where it becomes a first-order condition.
result: They prove that the weak c-cyclical monotonicity property characterizes optimal transport plans under suitable assumptions, recovering classical results with new proofs.
conclusion: The work sheds new light on monotonicity concepts in optimal transport, bridging classical and weak formulations.

title: Renormalisation Techniques For Inflation Systems And Some Of Their Applications
authors: Michael Baake, Franz G\"ahler, Anna Klick, Neil Ma\~nibo, Jan Maz\'a\v{c}
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19645v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exact renormalisation techniques are important and powerful, particularly for inflation-generated systems. We review recent results in this direction. We recall the necessary notions for inflation systems and show the renormalisation principle, which allows us to obtain exact values of highly erratic functions, such as window covariograms. We apply these techniques to compute the diffraction pattern of the new monotile tilings with arbitrary precision. We also recall a recent invariant for system with pure-point spectrum, the orbit separation dimension, and its relation to renormalisation. Lastly, we recall results beyond the pure-point spectrum setting and show how renormalisation and Lyapunov exponents can be used to exclude the presence of absolutely continuous part of the spectra.
tldr: This paper reviews renormalisation techniques for inflation systems and applies them to compute diffraction patterns of monotile tilings.
motivation: To develop exact renormalisation methods for inflation-generated systems and demonstrate their utility in computing highly erratic functions like window covariograms.
method: The authors recall necessary notions for inflation systems, present a renormalisation principle, and apply it to compute diffraction patterns with arbitrary precision. They also discuss the orbit separation dimension and use Lyapunov exponents to exclude absolutely continuous spectral components.
result: Exact values of window covariograms are obtained, and diffraction patterns of new monotile tilings are computed precisely. The orbit separation dimension is related to renormalisation, and Lyapunov exponents help rule out absolutely continuous spectra.
conclusion: Renormalisation techniques are powerful for inflation systems, enabling exact computations and spectral analysis beyond pure-point spectrum settings.

title: Sft-wick: A Formalism And Package For Feynman-diagram Expansion And Evaluation In Stochastic Field Theories
authors: Zheng Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19480v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When stochastic field dynamics are cast into a path-integral formulation, perturbation theory becomes systematic but the resulting expansion quickly grows combinatorially large. The setting targeted here includes multi-component, multi-dimensional fields with matrix propagators, tensor-valued couplings, and non-Gaussian driving noise specified by arbitrary [MATH]-point cumulants. Wick pairings grow factorially, and component indices must be routed through the tensor-valued vertices. The useful output is not a raw contraction list, but a diagram table: one entry per topology, with multiplicities, coupling sums, signs, and causal constraints resolved. We present sft-wick, an open-source Python package that constructs these diagram tables and computes their integrals numerically. Given an action and an observable, it enumerates topologically distinct Feynman diagrams, derives their algebraic coefficients, and evaluates the resulting diagram integrals from user-supplied response and cumulant functions. The core algorithm enumerates spatial topologies before routing component indices, avoiding contraction-by-contraction Wick expansion. Response-field constraints, including vanishing response-response contractions, the ito prescription, and the absence of causal response loops, are enforced during enumeration. Predictions are validated against direct Langevin simulation, agreeing to within the simulation's statistical noise.
tldr: A formalism and Python package for Feynman diagram expansion in stochastic field theories.
motivation: Stochastic field theories suffer from combinatorial explosion in perturbation theory; a systematic tool is needed to enumerate and evaluate diagrams.
method: The package enumerates topologically distinct Feynman diagrams by separating spatial topology from component index routing, enforcing response-field constraints.
result: Validated against direct Langevin simulation, predictions agree within statistical noise.
conclusion: Sft-wick provides an efficient automated tool for perturbative calculations in stochastic field theories.

title: Universal Properties Of Nonlinearly Perturbed Maxwell Theory
authors: Yisong Yang Tengyang Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that a general nonlinearly perturbed Maxwell theory of electromagnetism possesses three universal fundamental properties: (i) A finite-energy electric point charge. (ii) Exclusion of finite-energy magnetic monopoles and dually charged dyons. (iii) Arbitrary smallness of the effective radius of a point electric charge and the associated local undetectedness of the electric charge and energy. In particular, this last property offers a classical explanation for the invisibility of the electron, as a point electric charge, in accordance with the smallness of its effective radius. This nonlinear theory of electromagnetism has the feature that it minimally perturbs the Maxwell theory with a nonlinearity profile that is as general as possible such that the three universal properties stated above are all maintained.
tldr: A classical nonlinear perturbation of Maxwell theory yields finite-energy point charges, excludes magnetic monopoles, and explains the electron's small effective radius.
motivation: To understand whether nonlinear corrections to Maxwell's equations can resolve classical singularities and explain properties of elementary particles.
method: The authors consider a general nonlinear Lagrangian density that minimally perturbs Maxwell theory and derive conditions for finite-energy solutions, then analyze the existence of monopoles and the effective radius of point charges.
result: The theory supports finite-energy electric point charges, forbids finite-energy magnetic monopoles and dyons, and allows arbitrarily small effective radii for electric charges.
conclusion: The nonlinear Maxwell theory provides a classical mechanism for the invisibility of the electron's point charge, but the work is purely classical and unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A Unified Resource-pool Architecture For High-dimensional Direct-detection Optical Communication
authors: Jingze Liu, Zhijuan Gu, Xinyang Yu, Ziwen Zhou, Zhuyixiao Liu, Mingming Zhang, Yuxuan Xiong, Peng Li, Zhongyao Luo1, Jiajie Yuan, Hao Wu, Zhipei Sun, Siqi Yan, Yu Yu, Ming Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Increasing optical communication capacity without proportionally increasing receiver complexity remains a key challenge for direct-detection links. Conventional systems typically assign wavelength, polarization and intensity to fixed, separately recovered functions, so that alphabet expansion is accompanied by additional demultiplexing, polarization handling, receiver branches and electronic processing. Here we introduce a unified resource-pool architecture for high-dimensional direct-detection optical communication, in which wavelength, polarization and intensity are jointly organized as a composite optical symbol space and recovered through optical-domain joint projection rather than dimension-by-dimension separation. The receiver is implemented with an integrated disordered photonic processor that transforms each composite optical state into a reproducible multi-output electrical fingerprint for single-shot direct recovery. In a dual-wavelength transmission experiment, the system resolves 4096 composite symbols, corresponding to 12 bits per symbol slot, with a bit error rate of 4.25e-4 after 10 km standard-fiber transmission. Additional experiments demonstrate dense polarization alphabets, wavelength-indexed state-space expansion and high-launch-power operation over hollow-core fiber. These results establish disorder-enabled joint projection in an integrated photonic processor as a route to hardware-efficient high-dimensional direct-detection communication beyond conventional dimension-partitioned receiver architecture.
tldr: This paper presents a unified resource-pool architecture for high-dimensional direct-detection optical communication using an integrated disordered photonic processor.
motivation: Increasing optical communication capacity without proportionally increasing receiver complexity is a key challenge for direct-detection links.
method: The authors introduce a unified resource-pool architecture where wavelength, polarization, and intensity are jointly organized as composite optical symbols and recovered via optical-domain joint projection using an integrated disordered photonic processor.
result: In a dual-wavelength transmission experiment, the system resolves 4096 composite symbols (12 bits per symbol slot) with a bit error rate of 4.25e-4 after 10 km standard-fiber transmission.
conclusion: Disorder-enabled joint projection in an integrated photonic processor offers a hardware-efficient route to high-dimensional direct-detection communication beyond conventional dimension-partitioned receiver architectures.

title: Dirac Structures On Tangent Bundles: A Geometric Framework For Variational Principles, Constrained Dynamics, And Symmetry Reduction
authors: Hiroaki Yoshimura
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a Dirac structure on the tangent bundle of a configuration manifold, called a , which is naturally induced by the Lagrangian two-form associated with a (possibly degenerate) Lagrangian and a constraint distribution. This structure provides a unified geometric framework for Lagrange--Dirac dynamical systems, encompassing nonholonomic, degenerate Lagrangian, and symmetric systems. In the hyperregular case, the system recovers a first-order formulation of the Lagrange--d'Alembert equations. Although nonholonomic dynamics does not preserve the Lagrangian two-form, we show that the underlying Lagrange--Dirac structure is preserved up to gauge transformations, yielding a natural gauge covariance property. We also formulate an intrinsic variational principle directly on the tangent bundle, referred to as the , which recovers Hamilton's principle in the unconstrained case and the Lagrange--d'Alembert principle in the hyperregular constrained case. Furthermore, we develop a reduction theory for systems with Lie group symmetry, deriving a reduced Lagrange--Dirac structure over the Lie algebra that yields the Euler--Poincar\'e--Dirac equations and a corresponding reduced variational principle. Finally, we illustrate the theory through examples including charged particles, electric circuits, and systems with Lagrangians linear in velocity, and present an infinite-dimensional extension to ideal fluids that naturally incorporates the incompressibility constraint and recovers the Euler equations.
tldr: Introduces a Dirac structure on tangent bundles for a unified geometric framework of constrained Lagrangian systems, including nonholonomic and degenerate cases.
motivation: To provide a unified geometric description for variational principles, constrained dynamics, and symmetry reduction in Lagrangian systems.
method: Defines a Dirac structure on the tangent bundle using the Lagrangian two-form and a constraint distribution, and develops reduction theory for Lie group symmetries.
result: Derives Lagrange-Dirac equations, a gauge covariance property, and a reduced variational principle; illustrates with examples like charged particles and ideal fluids.
conclusion: The framework successfully unifies various constrained dynamical systems and extends to infinite-dimensional systems such as fluids.

title: Extremal Representations Of Functions Of Matrices And Applications To Multivariate Prediction
authors: Michael Frank, Lutz Klotz, Andreas Lasarow
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by two seminal results of multivariate prediction theory by Helson and Lowdenslager and by Wiener and Masani we prove extremal representations of functions of matrices and derive their prediction-theoretic consequences. We also sketch a way to obtain matricial inequalities from our results. The main goal of the paper is the computation of the infimum of a set of values of the form [MATH], where [MATH] is a given non-negative Hermitian [MATH] matrix and the choices for [MATH] exhauste a certain set of [MATH] matrices. In particular, we focus on norm-bounded unit spheres with certain types of properties of unitary invariance, what allows an application of the theory of majorization.
tldr: The paper derives extremal representations of functions of matrices and applies them to multivariate prediction theory.
motivation: To compute infimums of certain matrix-valued expressions and derive prediction-theoretic consequences motivated by Helson-Lowdenslager and Wiener-Masani results.
method: Uses matrix analysis, majorization theory, and extremal representations to characterize infimums over norm-bounded unit spheres with unitary invariance.
result: Provides explicit extremal representations and matricial inequalities for multivariate prediction problems.
conclusion: The results offer a unified framework for certain matrix optimization problems in prediction theory.

title: Neural Architectures As Functional Priors In Physics-Informed Control Problems
authors: Sonia Rubio Herranz, Fernando Carlos L\'opez Hern\'andez, Antonio L\'opez Montes
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work we investigate the role of neural architectures as implicit functional priors in control problems governed by ordinary differential equations. Rather than focusing on highly complex problems, our objective is to investigate architecture-dependent effects in controlled dynamical systems within the simplest physically interpretable settings possible. In particular, we study a controlled linear RLC electrical circuit and a nonlinear Duffing-type dynamical system. Both systems are analyzed first through classical optimal-control formulations and later through PINN-based approaches. We compare different combinations of multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and Fourier-based KAN-like architectures, and analyze their influence on the resulting controls. The numerical experiments suggest that different architectural choices systematically generate qualitatively distinct controls, even under identical governing equations, loss functionals, initial and target states, training parameters and physical constraints. Significant differences appear in the spectral structure, smoothness, energy distribution, and phase-space behavior of the learned solutions. A central observation of this work is the emergence of a functional specialization phenomenon when the neural architectures are allowed sufficient freedom to shape the structure of the learned controls. More specifically, in the systems considered here, Fourier-based architectures tend to produce trajectories with richer oscillatory content, whereas smoother low-frequency-biased architectures tend to generate more regular and energetically efficient controls. This suggests that different functional components of the control problem may be handled more efficiently by different neural architectures, leading to an implicit specialization between state representation and control generation.
tldr: This paper studies how neural network architectures act as implicit functional priors in physics-informed control of ODE systems, focusing on architectural effects rather than quantum or thermodynamic aspects.
motivation: To understand how different neural architectures (MLPs vs. Fourier-based KAN) influence learned controls in simple dynamical systems, independent of problem complexity.
method: Compares classical optimal control with PINN-based approaches for a linear RLC circuit and a nonlinear Duffing oscillator, using MLPs and Fourier-based KAN architectures.
result: Fourier-based architectures produce oscillatory controls, while smoother architectures yield more regular, energy-efficient controls, indicating functional specialization.
conclusion: Neural architecture choice systematically shapes control solutions, suggesting implicit specialization between state representation and control generation.

title: Moreau-Yosida-based Kohn-Sham Inversion For Periodic Systems
authors: Vebj{\o}rn H. Bakkestuen, Michael F. Herbst, Vegard Falm{\aa}r, Markus Penz, Andre Laestadius
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Density-potential inversion for periodic systems within Moreau-Yosida-regularised density-functional theory is investigated, both theoretically and numerically. We develop the framework in a periodic homogeneous Sobolev space and use it to recover the exchange-correlation potential of Kohn-Sham theory through a limiting procedure. A key analytical ingredient is the proof of lower semicontinuity of the non-interacting kinetic-energy functional in the chosen topology. The proximal mapping, together with its algorithmic evaluation, plays a central role in the resulting inversion scheme. Numerical experiments illustrate the performance and properties of the method for both the Kohn-Sham and Gross-Pitaevskii equations.
tldr: This paper develops a density-potential inversion method for periodic systems using Moreau-Yosida regularization in density-functional theory.
motivation: To recover the exchange-correlation potential in Kohn-Sham theory for periodic systems, which is important for electronic structure calculations.
method: The authors formulate the inversion in a periodic homogeneous Sobolev space, prove lower semicontinuity of the non-interacting kinetic-energy functional, and use the proximal mapping in an algorithmic inversion scheme.
result: Numerical experiments demonstrate the method's performance for Kohn-Sham and Gross-Pitaevskii equations.
conclusion: The Moreau-Yosida regularization provides a rigorous and effective framework for density-potential inversion in periodic systems.

title: One-point Functions For $C_2$-cofinite VOAs: Pseudo-traces And Trace Spaces Of Projective Modules
authors: Max-Niklas Steffen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the space of one-point functions on the torus for a possibly nonrational [MATH]-cofinite vertex operator algebra [MATH] by relating it to a trace object of the subcategory of projective objects in the representation category of [MATH]. We identify the dual of the trace space with symmetric functions on the endomorphism algebra [MATH] of a projective generator. Motivated by the Gainutdinov-Runkel conjecture, recently established using different methods by Gui and Zhang, we present a complementary representation-theoretic approach based on Arike-Nagatomo pseudo-traces. In this framework, we prove surjectivity of the Gainutdinov-Runkel map from symmetric functions on [MATH] to one-point functions. Under the additional assumption of separated conformal weights modulo [MATH], we also prove injectivity, using projective-cover techniques inspired by Huang.
tldr: This paper studies one-point functions on the torus for nonrational vertex operator algebras using pseudo-traces and projective module trace spaces.
motivation: To understand the space of one-point functions for C2-cofinite vertex operator algebras, which is important in conformal field theory and representation theory.
method: Relates one-point functions to a trace object of projective modules, identifies the dual of the trace space with symmetric functions on the endomorphism algebra of a projective generator, and uses Arike-Nagatomo pseudo-traces.
result: Proves surjectivity of the Gainutdinov-Runkel map from symmetric functions to one-point functions, and injectivity under an additional assumption of separated conformal weights modulo integers.
conclusion: Provides a complementary representation-theoretic approach to the Gainutdinov-Runkel conjecture, confirming results obtained by other methods.

title: Mean-Field Control With A Common Hidden State Under Decentralized Observations
authors: Ali D. Kara Erhan Bayraktar
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study optimal control of a system with multiple decision makers who share a common hidden state and receive fully decentralized observations through identical channels. The dynamics of the hidden state and the cost incurred by the agents depend on the agents' actions only through their empirical distribution. In the limit problem with infinitely many agents, the problem reduces to a single agent control problem where the agent affects the hidden state dynamics via the conditional law of the actions given the past values of the hidden state process. We formulate this problem as a deterministic measure valued control problem over the space of policies and provide a dynamic programming recursion. We first show that for the limiting problem randomization over the control actions is necessary for optimality. However, randomization over the selection of policies (i.e., mixture policies) is not required. We then show that the optimal symmetric policies designed for the infinite population problem are near optimal for the finite population problem. In particular, we establish convergence rates that decay with number of agents as [MATH], and grow exponentially with the memory length used in the policy.
tldr: This paper studies mean-field control with decentralized observations and a common hidden state, focusing on optimal control and convergence rates for multi-agent systems.
motivation: To understand optimal control in large-scale multi-agent systems where agents have decentralized observations and a shared hidden state, with applications in distributed decision-making.
method: The authors formulate a deterministic measure-valued control problem over policy space, derive a dynamic programming recursion, and prove necessity of randomization over actions but not over policies, then establish convergence rates for finite populations.
result: Optimal symmetric policies for infinite population are near-optimal for finite populations, with convergence rates decaying as 1/sqrt(N) and exponential in memory length.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for mean-field control under decentralized observations, but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Explicit Fourier Integrator For The Periodic dNLS Via Gauge Transformation: Low-Regularity Estimates In Discrete Bourgain Spaces
authors: Lun Ji, Hang Li, Alexander Ostermann, Gangfan Zhong
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The derivative nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation is a fundamental model for the propagation of nonlinear dispersive waves in, for example, plasma physics and nonlinear optics. In this work, we consider this model on the one-dimensional torus and study a filtered explicit Fourier integrator for the corresponding periodic problem. After applying a periodic gauge transformation, we consider a frequency-truncated model and its filtered exponential-Euler discretization. The main difficulty comes from the derivative cubic nonlinearity in the periodic setting, since local smoothing is unavailable and resonant interactions are stronger than in the non-periodic case. To address this issue, we develop a discrete Bourgain-space framework adapted to the gauge-transformed equation. For initial data [MATH] with [MATH], we prove that the numerical error is of order [MATH] in [MATH], where [MATH] denotes the employed time step size. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence behavior and demonstrate the effectiveness of the filtered scheme for rough solutions.
tldr: This paper develops a filtered explicit Fourier integrator for the periodic derivative nonlinear Schrödinger equation using a gauge transformation and discrete Bourgain spaces, proving convergence for rough initial data.
motivation: To construct and analyze a numerical scheme for the periodic dNLS equation that handles derivative cubic nonlinearity and low-regularity initial data, where standard methods fail due to lack of local smoothing and strong resonant interactions.
method: Applies a periodic gauge transformation to simplify the nonlinearity, then introduces a frequency-truncated model and a filtered exponential-Euler discretization. A discrete Bourgain-space framework is developed to handle the periodic setting and prove error estimates.
result: Proves that the numerical error is of order O(τ^{1/2}) in H^1 for initial data in H^s with s > 1/2, where τ is the time step size. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence.
conclusion: The proposed filtered scheme is effective for solving the periodic dNLS equation with rough initial data, and the discrete Bourgain-space technique provides a robust framework for low-regularity error analysis.

title: Learning Neural Maximal Lyapunov Functions On $\mathsf{SO}(n)$
authors: Matthieu Barreau Adeel Akhtar
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Establishing stability guarantees for dynamical systems on Lie groups is a fundamental challenge, as classical Lyapunov methods developed for Euclidean spaces do not directly transfer to curved geometries. In this paper, we propose a framework for learning maximal Lyapunov functions for systems evolving on the special orthogonal group [MATH]. Theoretically, we introduce a neural Lyapunov architecture based on the logarithmic map with proven approximation capabilities, and we formulate the learning problem via a Zubov-type characterization of the maximal region of attraction. A key technical contribution is the derivation of explicit, numerically tractable formulas for the derivative of the logarithmic map, enabling training through a two-phase algorithm that balances computational efficiency and accuracy. Empirically, we validate the approach on a low-dimensional nonlinear system.
tldr: This paper proposes a neural network framework for learning maximal Lyapunov functions on the special orthogonal group SO(n) to certify stability of dynamical systems on Lie groups.
motivation: Classical Lyapunov methods for Euclidean spaces do not directly apply to curved geometries like Lie groups, so a new approach is needed to establish stability guarantees for systems evolving on such manifolds.
method: The authors introduce a neural Lyapunov architecture using the logarithmic map on SO(n), derive explicit formulas for its derivative, and formulate the learning problem via a Zubov-type characterization of the maximal region of attraction, trained with a two-phase algorithm.
result: The approach is validated on a low-dimensional nonlinear system, demonstrating that the learned Lyapunov function accurately approximates the maximal region of attraction.
conclusion: The framework provides a principled way to learn Lyapunov functions on SO(n), with potential extensions to other Lie groups and applications in control theory.

title: Secure Coding Drift In LLM-Assisted Post-Quantum Cryptography Development: A Gamified Fix
authors: R. D. N. Shakya, C. P. Wijesiriwardana, S. M. Vidanagamachchi, Nalin A. G. Arachchilage
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The transition to Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC) introduces considerable implementation complexity, requiring strict adherence to constant-time execution, side channel resistance, and precise parametrisation. Simultaneously, large language models (LLMs) are heavily embedded in software development workflows, including cryptographic engineering. While LLMs improve productivity, evidence shows that they frequently generate insecure or suboptimal code, particularly in security critical domains. This paper introduces Secure Coding Drift in PQC, a novel socio technical vulnerability model capturing the gradual degradation of secure coding practices due to sustained reliance on LLM-generated code. Unlike prior work that focuses on static vulnerabilities, we conceptualise security risk as a longitudinal behavioural phenomenon rising from human AI interaction. To mitigate this, we propose a gamified, LLM augmented secure coding framework that embeds adversarial evaluation, behavioural feedback, and security scoring into development workflows. Our approach reframes LLMs from passive assistants into active security co-pilots, contributing toward safer PQC implementation in AI mediated environments.
tldr: This paper introduces a socio-technical vulnerability model for secure coding drift in post-quantum cryptography development due to LLM assistance, and proposes a gamified framework to mitigate it.
motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in cryptographic engineering but often generate insecure code, posing risks for PQC implementation.
method: The authors conceptualize 'Secure Coding Drift' as a longitudinal behavioral phenomenon and design a gamified, LLM-augmented framework with adversarial evaluation and security scoring.
result: The framework aims to transform LLMs from passive assistants into active security co-pilots, improving secure coding practices in PQC.
conclusion: The work contributes to safer PQC implementation in AI-mediated environments by addressing human-AI interaction risks.

title: Design Considerations For Phase Modulation In Testable Photonic Systems And Co-packaged Optics
authors: Pratishtha Agnihotri, Priyank Kalla, Steve Blair
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19674v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As silicon photonic integrated circuits (PICs) scale in complexity, testing and calibration increasingly depend on effective phase modulation mechanisms. This work compares thermally induced phase modulation and carrier-based electrical modulation in Mach-Zehnder and microring modulators. The devices are designed and evaluated for extinction ratio, tuning efficiency, power consumption, and modulation bandwidth. The study identifies key trade-offs among modulation speed, energy consumption, and tuning controllability that directly influence the suitability of these methods for test signal generation and calibration tasks. The results highlight the relative advantages and limitations of thermal and electrical approaches across different operating regimes. These findings provide practical design guidance for selecting phase modulation strategies in scalable silicon photonic systems with integrated test and calibration requirements.
tldr: This paper compares thermal and electrical phase modulation in silicon photonic integrated circuits for testing and calibration.
motivation: Scalable silicon photonic circuits require effective phase modulation for testing and calibration, but the trade-offs between thermal and electrical methods are not well characterized.
method: The authors design and simulate Mach-Zehnder and microring modulators, comparing thermally induced and carrier-based electrical modulation in terms of extinction ratio, tuning efficiency, power consumption, and bandwidth.
result: Thermal modulation offers high tuning efficiency and controllability but low speed and high power, while electrical modulation provides higher speed and lower power but lower efficiency and more complex control.
conclusion: The choice between thermal and electrical phase modulation depends on the specific requirements of speed, energy, and controllability for test signal generation and calibration in silicon photonic systems.

title: Image Encryption Algorithm Based On Convolutional Neural Networks And Dynamic S-Box Generation
authors: Ans Ibrahim, Fadhil Abbas Fadhil, Mahameed Reza Feizi Derakhshi, Maryam Mahdi Alhusseini, Nikolai Safiullin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The paper proposes a dynamic approach to image encryption, combining the use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and classical cryptography to improve the security and flexibility of image encryption. The main concept is to create adaptive Substitution boxes (S-boxes) based on characteristics that are learned by a trained CNN. The CNN-based S-boxes can be relied on for more non-linearity, uniqueness, and input image dependence than the conventional fixed S-boxes because they are susceptible to the linear and differential attacks. This dynamic behaviour enhances the confusion property and makes it more resistant to statistical and structural attacks. The encryption algorithm consists of CNN-based feature extraction and the creation of a personalised S-box to replace the pixels. Entropy, histogram analysis, correlation, NPCR, and UACI enable security assessment of generated S-boxes based on the CNN, indicating that the scheme is more resilient and flexible than traditional ones.
tldr: This paper proposes an image encryption algorithm using CNNs to generate dynamic S-boxes, combining classical cryptography with deep learning.
motivation: To improve image encryption security by making S-boxes adaptive and input-dependent, thereby resisting linear and differential attacks better than fixed S-boxes.
method: A CNN extracts features from the input image and generates a personalized S-box, which is then used in a substitution-permutation network for encryption.
result: Security metrics (entropy, histogram, correlation, NPCR, UACI) show the scheme is more resilient and flexible than traditional methods.
conclusion: The dynamic CNN-based S-box approach enhances confusion and resistance to statistical and structural attacks.

title: Calling The Brane Next Door: The Kaluza-Klein Tower As A Gravitational Information Channel
authors: Karim Benakli
abstract: ArXiv:2606.09969v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Could two worlds localised on neighbouring branes communicate through gravity alone? We investigate this question in a minimal higher-dimensional framework in which Standard Model fields are confined to our brane while gravity propagates through the bulk. From the brane-to-brane graviton propagator we derive the retarded transfer kernel of the inter-brane link and identify the transition from evanescent to propagating Kaluza-Klein modes. The central idea is to give the Kaluza-Klein tower a new role: not only as a spectrum of massive gravitational states, but as a set of communication carriers. Below the first KK threshold the channel is effectively four-dimensional and is mediated only by the massless graviton. Above threshold, massive KK modes open as additional propagating subchannels, and information may be encoded in their occupation pattern, relative phases, and arrival-time structure as well as in ordinary signal variables. The compactification determines the KK masses, wavefunctions, brane overlap factors, and propagation phases, which together define a multi-input multi-output (MIMO) channel matrix. In the resolved-mode limit, the tower yields approximate parallel subchannels, to which standard information-theoretic notions such as capacity bounds, water-filling, effective rank, and sparse occupancy codes apply. The production and detection of such signals are highly model-dependent and not assumed to be feasible with known technology. Nevertheless, the channel structure is well defined: a neighbouring brane-world could be separated from us by a microscopic distance in the compact space while remaining hidden because the only shared interaction is gravity. The first observable signature may not be a deliberate message, but the spectral and modal structure of the Kaluza-Klein tower itself, revealing partial information about the geometry of a nearby hidden world.
tldr: This paper explores using Kaluza-Klein modes as communication carriers between branes in a higher-dimensional framework, applying information-theoretic concepts to gravitational signaling.
motivation: To investigate whether two brane-worlds separated in a compact extra dimension could communicate solely via gravity, and to characterize the resulting information channel.
method: The authors derive the retarded transfer kernel from the brane-to-brane graviton propagator, identify evanescent and propagating KK modes, and model the channel as a MIMO system with subchannels defined by KK masses, wavefunctions, and brane overlaps.
result: Below the first KK threshold the channel is 4D and mediated only by the massless graviton; above threshold, massive KK modes open as additional subchannels, enabling information encoding in occupation patterns, phases, and arrival times.
conclusion: The KK tower can serve as a set of communication carriers, and the channel structure is well-defined even if practical detection is infeasible; the first observable signature may be the spectral structure of the KK tower itself.

title: Record Nonlinear Conversion Efficiency In The Production Of High Spectral Purity Vacuum Ultraviolet Laser At 148 Nm
authors: Sergey Vasilyev, Tian Ooi, Igor Moskalev, Mike Mirov, Andrey Muraviev, Dmitrii Konnov, Victor Churikov, Viktor Sukharev, Evgeny Galenin1, Jack F. Doyle, Chuankun Zhang, Kai Li, Georgiy Seryogin, Dan Perlov, Igor Samartsev, Konstantin Vodopyanov, Jun Ye
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coherent vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) lasers are indispensable for precision measurement, quantum optics, and materials science. Recent high-resolution spectroscopy of the Th-229 nuclear clock transition near 148 nm highlights the urgent demand for intense, narrow-linewidth VUV lasers for advancing metrology and testing fundamental physics. However, existing VUV generation schemes typically require enhancement cavities [C. Zhang et al., Opt. Lett. 47, 5591-5594 (2022)], atomic resonances [Q. Xiao et al., Nature 650, 852-856 (2026)], or random quasi-phase-matched nonlinear crystals [V. Lal et al., Optica 12, 1971-1974 (2025)]. Here, we demonstrate a VUV frequency comb via cascaded frequency doubling of a 2400 nm Cr:ZnS comb to its 16th harmonic in nonlinear crystals. The final stage employs a bulk-grown, spatially uniform quasi-phase matched (QPM) crystal developed by IPG, combining VUV transparency, high [MATH] nonlinearity, and power scalability. Using this QPM crystal we generate a VUV frequency comb with 40 [MATH]W average power (1 nW per mode at 80 MHz mode spacing) with a conversion efficiency order of magnitude higher than other known methods. These results establish a scalable route to compact VUV sources via direct frequency doubling, opening a path toward a robust continuous-wave nuclear clock laser.
tldr: This paper demonstrates record nonlinear conversion efficiency for generating vacuum ultraviolet laser light at 148 nm using cascaded frequency doubling and a quasi-phase-matched crystal.
motivation: There is a need for intense, narrow-linewidth VUV lasers for precision measurement, quantum optics, and nuclear clock spectroscopy, but existing methods have low efficiency or require complex setups.
method: The authors use a 2400 nm Cr:ZnS frequency comb and cascade frequency doubling to its 16th harmonic, with the final stage employing a bulk-grown, spatially uniform quasi-phase-matched nonlinear crystal.
result: They achieve 40 μW average power (1 nW per mode at 80 MHz) with conversion efficiency an order of magnitude higher than other known methods.
conclusion: This work establishes a scalable route to compact VUV sources via direct frequency doubling, enabling robust continuous-wave nuclear clock lasers.

title: TorchNEP: Ultra-Efficient And Accurate Training Of Neuroevolution Potentials
authors: Yong-Chao Wu, Xiaoya Chang, Tero M\"akinen, Amin Esfandiarpour, Jian-Li Shao, Tapio Ala-Nissila, Zheyong Fan, Mikko Alava
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neuroevolution Potential (NEP) is one of the most efficient machine-learned interatomic potential frameworks for large-scale atomistic simulations. However, its original training strategy remains computationally demanding, limiting systematic exploration of model architectures and training protocols. Here, we present TorchNEP, a PyTorch-based implementation of NEP that combines analytically derived gradients, adaptive optimization, and a two-stage training strategy. TorchNEP accelerates training by more than two orders of magnitude while maintaining full compatibility with existing NEP models. We further show that the improvement in predictive accuracy primarily originates from the two-stage training protocol rather than the optimization algorithm itself. Across diverse benchmark datasets, TorchNEP consistently improves force and stress predictions while maintaining comparable or improved energy accuracy. Benchmark evaluations on elemental and alloy systems demonstrate enhanced predictive performance for both atomic configurations and key materials properties. Furthermore, we show that increasing model complexity does not necessarily improve predictive performance despite reducing training errors. Overall, TorchNEP provides an efficient and flexible training framework for developing more accurate and robust machine-learned interatomic potentials.
tldr: TorchNEP is a PyTorch-based implementation of Neuroevolution Potentials that accelerates training by over two orders of magnitude while improving predictive accuracy.
motivation: The original NEP training strategy is computationally demanding, limiting systematic exploration of model architectures and training protocols.
method: The authors implement NEP in PyTorch with analytically derived gradients, adaptive optimization, and a two-stage training strategy.
result: TorchNEP accelerates training by more than 100x, and the two-stage training protocol significantly improves force and stress predictions across diverse benchmarks.
conclusion: TorchNEP provides an efficient and flexible framework for developing more accurate machine-learned interatomic potentials, but increasing model complexity does not necessarily improve performance.

title: Alignment-Controlled Optical Orbital Trapping Of Single Airborne Aerosols For Dynamical Particle Sensing
authors: Chun-Yen Wen, Yang-Yi Lee, Chung-Lin Chao, Ruei-Ying Jian, Wayne Cheng-Wei Huang, Tzu-Ling Chen*
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical forces in focused-beam traps are generally nonconservative, yet the controlled use of this nonconservative component for airborne single-particle dynamics remains limited. We demonstrate a dual-beam optical trap in which a single aerosol can be switched between localized confinement and sustained orbital motion by tuning the relative positions of two counter-propagating foci. The axial separation controls the onset of nonconservative circulation, while the lateral offset tunes the projected orbit size and causes a monotonic change in the rotation frequency. T-matrix optical force calculations and Langevin simulations support this interpretation by showing that finite axial misalignment activates a circulating force component, whereas near-zero axial separation gives a confinement-dominated force field. Experiments confirm the predicted switching behavior through mean-square displacement and frequency measurements. We further show that the projected orbit geometry provides a particle-dependent observable, with the orbit anisotropy Ay/Ax varying systematically with aerosol diameter. The results provide a compact, low-power platform for controlled orbital dynamics of single airborne particles and for future aerosol measurements based on nonequilibrium trajectory observables.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a dual-beam optical trap for controlling orbital motion of single airborne aerosols, with applications in particle sensing.
motivation: To exploit nonconservative optical forces for controlled dynamics of airborne particles, which has been limited.
method: Dual-beam optical trap with tunable axial and lateral offsets; T-matrix calculations and Langevin simulations support experiments.
result: Switching between confinement and orbital motion is achieved by adjusting axial separation; orbit anisotropy depends on particle diameter.
conclusion: Provides a compact platform for controlled orbital dynamics and aerosol sensing based on nonequilibrium trajectory observables.

title: \mu-MOPA Architecture For Photonic Integrated Solid State Laser
authors: Yu Guo, Yubo Wang, Haoqi Zhao, Fengyan Yang, Guangcanlan Yang, Hao Xie, Hong X. Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19768v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diode-pumped solid-state (DPSS) lasers play a central role in modern photonics owing to their exceptional efficiency and ability to extend spectral coverage beyond the reach of semiconductor diodes. These attributes have enabled breakthroughs in precision metrology, quantum optics, and coherent communications. However, bringing the proven advantages of DPSS gain media such as Nd:YAG onto an integrated photonic platform has remained difficult, largely due to inefficient pump utilization and limited power-scaling in chip-scale implementations. Here, we demonstrate the first photonic-integrated Nd:YAG laser-amplifier system that overcomes these challenges with a micro-chip based master-oscillator-power-amplifier (\mu-MOPA) architecture. The seed laser, employing a double-resonant microring resonator, could reach a threshold as low as 2.9 \mu W. The single-pass waveguide amplifier, when optimized separately, provides up to 46.6 dB small-signal gain. Combining the low-threshold seed with cascaded waveguide amplifiers, the integrated \mu-MOPA delivers more than 12 dBm of amplified continuous-wave output power. These results establish Nd:YAG waveguide integration as a practical route to compact and high-performance solid-state light sources.
tldr: Demonstrates a photonic-integrated Nd:YAG laser-amplifier system using a micro-chip master-oscillator-power-amplifier architecture.
motivation: To bring the advantages of DPSS lasers (e.g., Nd:YAG) onto an integrated photonic platform, overcoming challenges of inefficient pump utilization and limited power scaling.
method: A μ-MOPA architecture combining a double-resonant microring seed laser with cascaded single-pass waveguide amplifiers.
result: Achieved a seed laser threshold as low as 2.9 μW, 46.6 dB small-signal gain, and over 12 dBm amplified continuous-wave output power.
conclusion: Establishes Nd:YAG waveguide integration as a practical route to compact, high-performance solid-state light sources.

title: The Heat Kernel Expansion: Curvature For Shock Detection In Higher-Order Financial Networks
authors: Sara Najem Mohammad Elsayed
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work follows the evolution of financial networks in Norway over a period of nine years at a monthly rate. The data consist of board directors and their affiliations to companies, which we model as simplicial complexes. In this framework, directors are represented as nodes and companies as faces of the complex. To characterize the latter, we focus on three topological measures: the Euler characteristic, computed through the Betti numbers, torsion computed through the reduced determinant of the higher-order Laplacians, and higher-order clustering coefficients. The first two fail to capture the effect of imposed law on representation, unlike our notion of curvature which is a geometrical measure computed from the coefficients of the series expansion of the heat kernel in powers of time, which is our major contribution in this work. In particular, the Euler characteristic integrates curvature, and thus local information is lost. Subsequently, not every topological measure can reliably capture shocks in networks. Further, the number of spanning trees may undergo significant changes at the lowest order, yet these changes need not be reflected in the torsion. Conversely, the change in the curvature revealed variation in the board interlock due to legislation, and serves as a sensitive measure for detecting shocks in networks. Inflection points in curvature are associated with external forcing, and minima with shock arrival times. Sharp transitions are also observed in the components of torsion, while smooth changes are observed in higher-order clustering.
tldr: This paper applies heat kernel expansion and curvature to detect shocks in financial networks modeled as simplicial complexes.
motivation: To find a sensitive topological measure for detecting external shocks in financial networks, as traditional measures like Euler characteristic and torsion fail to capture legislative changes.
method: Financial networks are modeled as simplicial complexes; curvature is computed from the heat kernel expansion coefficients and compared with Euler characteristic, torsion, and higher-order clustering coefficients.
result: Curvature reveals variation in board interlock due to legislation and serves as a sensitive shock detector, with inflection points associated with external forcing and minima with shock arrival times.
conclusion: Curvature from heat kernel expansion is a more sensitive measure for shock detection in higher-order financial networks than traditional topological measures.

title: A 3d Passive Ring Gyroscope For Seismology
authors: Thomas Gereons, Jannik Zenner, Thorsten Groh, Simon Stellmer
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19976v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In seismology and related fields, the measurement of rotation in all three spatial dimensions is essential to complement the observation of translations. Access to all six degrees of freedom allows for full reconstruction of seismic wavefields and improves the understanding of complex ground motion during seismic events. In this regard, Sagnac interferometers in the form of large active ring laser systems have demonstrated remarkable performance. So-called passive ring gyroscopes offer the potential to bypass some of the limitations of active ring lasers and could represent a promising complement to existing sensor technology. Here, we present a prototype of a transportable three dimensional free-space passive ring gyroscope, reaching a sensitivity in the micro rad/s/sqrt(Hz) regime in all spatial dimensions. We demonstrate the sensor performance by reconstructing the rotational components of a simulated seismic event.
tldr: A transportable 3D passive ring gyroscope for seismology is presented, achieving micro rad/s/√Hz sensitivity.
motivation: Seismology requires measurement of all three rotational components to fully reconstruct seismic wavefields; active ring lasers are large and limited, so a passive ring gyroscope offers a more compact alternative.
method: A free-space passive ring gyroscope with three orthogonal axes is built and characterized; its sensitivity is measured and a simulated seismic event is reconstructed.
result: The prototype reaches micro rad/s/√Hz sensitivity in all three spatial dimensions and successfully reconstructs rotational components of a simulated earthquake.
conclusion: Passive ring gyroscopes can complement active ring lasers for rotational seismology, offering transportability and adequate sensitivity.

title: Noncommutative Cauchy Bound And Noncommutative Montel Bound For Roots Of Polynomials
authors: K. Mahesh Krishna
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 1829, Cauchy derived an upper bound for every root of a complex polynomial using the maximum of the absolute values of the coefficients. In 1931, Montel derived an upper bound using the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients. We derive noncommutative versions of the Cauchy and Montel bounds.
tldr: The paper derives noncommutative versions of classical Cauchy and Montel bounds for roots of polynomials, focusing on operator algebras.
motivation: Classical bounds for polynomial roots are extended to noncommutative settings, which may have applications in operator theory.
method: The authors adapt Cauchy's and Montel's bounds to polynomials with coefficients in a noncommutative algebra, using norms and spectral radii.
result: Noncommutative analogues of the Cauchy and Montel bounds are established.
conclusion: The work provides new bounds for roots of noncommutative polynomials, but its connection to quantum information or thermodynamics is not evident.

title: Fuzzy Owl 2 Reasoning: A Re-Engineered Python Framework
authors: Fernando Bobillo, Giuseppe Filippone, Gianmarco la Rosa, Umberto Straccia, Marco Elio Tabacchi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many real-world domains, knowledge is inherently vague or imprecise - features that classical ontology languages, based on crisp Description Logics (DLs), are unable to capture. This shortcoming poses particular challenges for applications in the Semantic Web and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), where robust reasoning over graded information is essential. Fuzzy ontologies address this limitation by enriching DLs with fuzzy logic, enabling the expression of partial truth and supporting more nuanced modelling of real-world knowledge. We present fuzzy-dl-owl2, a complete re-engineering in Python of the fuzzyDL reasoner and the Fuzzy OWL 2 framework. The former is an expressive fuzzy DL reasoner, while the latter allows for defining fuzzy ontologies within OWL 2. Our contribution addresses several shortcomings of the original software, including semantic inconsistencies, rigid architectural design, and limited solver integration. The re-implementation features a modular class hierarchy tailored for extensibility, supports a broader range of Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solvers (including open-source alternatives), and corrects IRI ambiguities arising from overlapping ontological elements. Furthermore, a dedicated Python library (pyowl2) has also been developed to handle OWL 2 annotations in a standards-compliant manner, improving interoperability with existing Semantic Web tooling and resolving IRI ambiguities. The resulting framework offers a portable, extensible, and theoretically grounded platform for reasoning with fuzzy ontologies, suitable for both research and deployment in vague-aware systems. Performance tests have also been conducted that show improved execution times w.r.t. the original Java implementation. The source code and full documentation are publicly available to facilitate community adoption and further development.
tldr: This paper presents a re-engineered Python framework for fuzzy ontology reasoning, addressing limitations of the original Java-based fuzzyDL reasoner.
motivation: Classical ontology languages cannot handle vague or imprecise knowledge, which is common in real-world domains like Semantic Web and XAI.
method: The authors re-implemented the fuzzyDL reasoner and Fuzzy OWL 2 framework in Python with a modular class hierarchy, support for multiple MILP solvers, and a new pyowl2 library for OWL 2 annotation handling.
result: The new framework corrects semantic inconsistencies, improves extensibility, supports open-source solvers, and shows improved execution times compared to the original Java implementation.
conclusion: The re-engineered framework provides a portable, extensible, and theoretically grounded platform for reasoning with fuzzy ontologies, suitable for research and deployment.

title: Corrigendum: Order Extreme Points And Solid Convex Hulls
authors: Anastasiia Ianina, Timur Oikhberg, Mary Angelica Tursi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We correct some errors found in [T. Oikhberg and M.A. Tursi, Order extreme points and solid convex hulls, in ``The Mathematical Legacy of Victor Lomonosov'' (ed. R. Aron et.al.), de Gryuter, 2020, 297--315.].
tldr: This is a corrigendum correcting errors in a previous paper on order extreme points and solid convex hulls in functional analysis.
motivation: The authors needed to correct errors found in their earlier work on order extreme points and solid convex hulls.
method: The paper lists specific corrections to the original text, equations, and proofs.
result: Errors in the original paper are corrected, ensuring the mathematical results are accurate.
conclusion: The corrigendum resolves the identified issues, maintaining the validity of the original work.

title: Lightweight Non-Line-of-Sight Channel Detection For ML-assisted Bluetooth Direction Finding
authors: Hamed Talebian, Aamir Mahmood, Mehdi Haghshenas, Stefani Rydbloom, Peter Karlsson, Mikael Gidlund
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) direction-finding is promising for indoor industrial localization, but its accuracy degrades in multipath environments where reflections and scattering bias angle estimates. Although line-of-sight (LOS) and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) detection is well studied for wide-band radios, BLE direction-finding still lacks narrow-band channel-feature representations, scalable kernel-based feature transformations, and dedicated datasets for data-driven, lightweight channel classification. To address this gap, the work introduces a controlled BLE measurement setup that generates labeled LOS/NLOS data in two distinct propagation environments. A quality-driven machine learning (ML)-based pipeline is then developed for BLE Constant Tone Extension (CTE) In-phase-Quadrature (IQ) features. First, robust quantile-based standardization is applied to reduce the influence of outliers and heavy-tailed effects. The standardized features are then analyzed using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Adaptive Kernel Density Estimation (AKDE) to verify scenario-dependent statistics and reveal LOS/NLOS separability. Next, Nystr\"om Kernel Approximation (NKA) constructs low-rank nonlinear feature maps followed by a lightweight Support Vector Classifier (SVC) head for LOS/NLOS detection. This classifier is compared with Random Forest (RF) and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) models. Results show that NKA improves accuracy by about 7-14% relative to the raw baseline. Although the MLP achieves higher absolute accuracy, the Nystr\"om--SVC approach offers a more favorable trade-off between training complexity, inference cost, and memory footprint. Finally, several pipeline-calibrated posterior probabilities are utilized for cost-aware threshold selection and efficient real-time LOS/NLOS detection in resource-constrained localization systems.
tldr: This paper presents a machine learning pipeline for LOS/NLOS channel detection in BLE direction-finding, focusing on narrow-band features and lightweight classifiers.
motivation: BLE direction-finding accuracy degrades in multipath environments; existing LOS/NLOS detection methods are designed for wide-band radios and lack narrow-band feature representations.
method: The authors collect labeled BLE IQ data in two environments, apply quantile-based standardization, PCA, and Adaptive Kernel Density Estimation for feature analysis, then use Nyström Kernel Approximation with an SVC head for classification, comparing with RF and MLP.
result: Nyström-SVC improves accuracy by 7-14% over raw baseline; MLP achieves higher accuracy but Nyström-SVC offers better trade-off in training complexity, inference cost, and memory.
conclusion: The proposed lightweight pipeline is suitable for real-time LOS/NLOS detection in resource-constrained localization systems.

title: Counterexample To A Conjecture On The Pairwise Independent Correlation Gap Using Ai
authors: Karthik Natarajan Arjun Ramachandra
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aided by the AI tool GPT5.5 Pro, we provide a counterexample to a conjecture made by Ramachandra and Natarajan (2025) [Pairwise independent correlation gap, Operations Research Letters, 107255, 6040].
tldr: Using an AI tool, the authors provide a counterexample to a conjecture about the pairwise independent correlation gap.
motivation: To disprove a previously made conjecture in the field of correlation gaps.
method: The authors used the AI tool GPT5.5 Pro to construct a counterexample.
result: A counterexample to the conjecture was found.
